title: From workflows to agentic automation with Azure Logic Apps | OD832

segments.text: [ Music ]
DIVYA SWARNKAR: Hello, everyone.
I'm Divya Swarnkar, Product Manager in Azure Logic Apps.
And today, I'm very excited to be here to talk
about how Logic Apps is evolving
from an enterprise-proven integration platform
to an AI automation platform.
We've got a lot of things to share today,
including a lot of demos.
So let's get into it.
So here is the agenda.
We have three parts to the session.
First, I'll talk about a brand new platform
that we are announcing at Build: Logic Apps Automation.
Second, we'll talk about knowledge
as a service capability,
where you can do managed RAG built directly
within the workflows.
And third, we'll talk about how Azure AI Foundry
and Logic Apps are coming together to build
and orchestrate real-world AI agents.
And yes, there are demos after every section.
So let's talk more about AI automation.
Before we talk about what's new, a quick grounding
in what Logic Apps platform already is.
It's a platform proven across a decade of enterprise use,
operating at planetary scale.
Today, the platform supports more
than 100,000 customers running millions of workflow executions
and trillions of connector operations every month.
And these span across more than 1,400 connectors connecting
to different SaaS applications, databases, AI services,
and on-prem applications.
The token usage and rapid growth, again,
comes from agentic workflows running
in production and at scale.
That matters because it tells us something important.
Customers, including most of Fortune 500 companies,
are already running enterprise workflows on Logic Apps
in production and at scale.
And it's not just scale.
It's everything you need to ship production-grade applications.
And that includes dedicated compute, VNet support, security,
identity networking, compliance
and all the other capabilities are required
to build enterprise-grade, production-ready application.
And these capabilities aren't supported as add-ons;
they are built into the platform from the start, from day zero.
And here is the part that matters today.
Every one of these enterprise foundations now extend to AI.
On top of the same platform foundations,
Logic Apps offers workflows and AI capabilities,
including agents, tools, human-in-the-loop controls.
So when customers ask us, "What's our path
from AI demo to production?"
Increasingly, the answer is they already have the platform they
can trust.
Because in production, success isn't just
about building intelligent agents;
it's about operating them reliably,
securely, and under governance.
And why having an enterprise platform matters.
Most companies at this point have built an AI agent demo,
but very few have one running in production.
Because for demos, the happy path is enough.
You don't need retries.
You don't need error handling.
You don't need logs.
However, in production, you need consistent outcomes.
You need the platform where networking, identity, security,
and governance are on from day one.
That's the distance between a demo or a prototype
and a business-critical workflow which requires governance.
And this is not magic.
Logic Apps, as a platform, is built for the right column.
But here is the catch.
The same things that make Logic Apps powerful and offers control
to the customers also makes it heavy to start.
There are multiple friction points.
Procurement process to get approvals
for multiple Azure services and AI models.
The provisioning and management overhead of the services
and the infrastructure.
And since these capabilities ship as separate Azure services,
you're wiring them together yourself,
and that sometimes can be the real cost.
Developers either burn weeks getting to the "hello,
world" or getting to the basic prototype,
or they pick a lighter-weight tool that doesn't actually fit,
but just because it's faster and easier to get started.
Either way, the platform we built isn't reaching the people
we need it most.
So why now?
Historically, automation was limited
by folks who could write code.
The people closest
to the business problems often couldn't build the solutions
themselves, which created the IT bottlenecks every company knows.
However, AI changes that dynamic.
Now, an operation lead, an analyst, an AI builder,
or a knowledge worker can describe a workflow
in natural language and actually participate in building it.
That's a massive shift.
Automation is no longer confined to central integration teams,
and that creates a clear need, a platform with power
and reliability to run production workloads,
but one that doesn't require you to be an Azure expert to use it.
That's the opportunity behind Logic Apps Automation.
So that's what we did.
We combined the two problems with two changes, and one thing
that we deliberately did not change.
Problem one was infrastructure overhead.
We took out the infrastructure management,
but we kept the Azure so that you get full Azure-grade
reliability and scale.
Problem two was the barrier to entry.
We took the Azure portal dependency out of the picture.
You can sign in with your Entra ID and start building.
No Azure access or expertise is required.
Yet, whatever you are building is being built on Azure.
These two things almost never come together.
They do now, and that's what led to this next announcement.
Today, we are introducing Azure Logic Apps Automation,
enterprise-ready automation platform built
for developers of every kind.
It offers low barrier to entry with the same enterprise rigor.
It's available in public preview today at auto.azure.com.
Four things that define this offering.
It's the same enterprise-ready platform that runs trillions
of action executions per month,
which means that it's production-ready from day one.
All your day zero friction goes away because all the compute,
infrastructure, and provisioning
of services is hosted on your behalf.
You sign in, and you're ready to build the workflows.
Thirdly, you don't need Azure portal to get started.
It's hosted outside Azure,
and all you need is Microsoft Entra ID to log in.
And fourthly, this is still built for enterprises.
All the production-ready
and enterprise controls are still built in.
You get isolated compute, RBAC, auditability, VNet support,
and everything else that Logic Apps
as an enterprise platform offers you today.
The goal was simple here.
We wanted to remove the friction, but not the rigor.
So let's see this in action through a demo.
SPEAKER 1: In this demo,
let's automate using Logic Apps Automation.
Remember those prerequisites we just talked about?
Watch what it takes to get started now.
I open my browser, go to auto.azure.com,
as it's hosted outside of Azure.
The landing page gives you a quick glimpse
into the product capabilities.
Let's sign in.
All you need is your Entra ID.
After login, you land in a page that shows all your projects.
Inside project, you can have one or more applications
and other shared resources like sandbox,
models, network policies.
Project admins can add developers to the projects
and give them permissions depending on their role
and required activity.
Let's talk about sandbox.
It's an isolated environment to run GitHub Copilot agents
with native file, shell, and web operations
with isolated execution.
These agents have native capabilities
to write code dynamically and support skills and MCPs
for their reasoning and actions.
The sandbox is configured at the project with repositories,
skills, and other context.
Inside a project, you have one or more applications.
Apps are where developers build.
Each app holds its workflows, connections, parameters,
and analytics dashboard, and its own permission model,
reader or contributor, so you can collaborate
without exposing the rest of the project.
Let's go ahead and create workflow inside the application.
So I'll first create my workflow
by describing it in natural language.
The agent will analyze this request and scaffold a workflow.
The generated workflow still needs its connections updated,
but a lot of the work is already taken care of by Copilot,
picking the connectors
and configuring many of the parameters.
From here, I can iteratively build and test the workflow
with Copilot's assistance.
When asked to write code, Copilot added the action
and wrote JavaScript code with appropriate exception handling.
Developers can make updates at the workflow scope or go
to the action scope and have Copilot make
action-specific updates.
We use a default LLM that's hosted for you,
but you can use your GitHub account to bring
in additional models, including both first-party
and third-party models.
Here's a workflow I've already built for invoice processing.
Real-world problems most of the time need to be solved
with a combination
of deterministic steps and AI reasoning.
That's the power of workflow automation here.
In this workflow, ServiceNow ticket creation
and Salesforce update are deterministic steps.
The invoice agent is provided a system prompt describing
its goals.
The agent here is built on the GitHub Copilot SDK and runs
on a sandbox, the isolated compute per workflow configured
at project.
The business context like invoice,
and skills for validation
and notification are provided to the agent here.
You can even provide GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories.
After the invoice validation process completes,
we again have a set of deterministic steps
to update Salesforce and close the ticket
if the invoice was approved.
Alongside the visual workflow,
the code view shows an editable view into the same workflow.
You can make updates in code view
and see the workflow update in real time.
Copilot assistant can be used here, too,
to write JavaScript expressions or code.
Being able to scope Copilot
to a specific action lets you make targeted,
action-specific updates.
Here, the agent is responding with code
in the scope of JavaScript action.
I can have multi-turn conversations
with agent to iterate over code.
When an invoice is received, the workflow triggers
and the run history shows full traceability
and auditability into every step.
With real-time streaming capabilities, you can view
into each step while it's happening.
For an agent node, you can visually see, in real time,
the tools it's using to accomplish tasks.
Every step of the workflow is logged with inputs and outputs,
execution time, and status.
Agent outcomes are logged,
including the token utilization at each step.
That's Logic Apps Automation.
Low barrier to entry with same enterprise rigor.
Preview is live today, and we can't wait
to see you build with it.
DIVYA SWARNKAR: So now that we have watched the demo,
let's take a quick look under the hood
so that we can understand the underlying model better.
The topmost construct is a project.
This is something where an admin operates.
You can think of projects as environments,
and these can be scoped by your development environments
or by your business domains.
It's up to you how you want to think about organization
of your business workflows.
Projects is how your platform
and infrastructure team controls access,
networking policies, and shared resources.
Inside a project, developers create applications,
one or multiple, however many they need.
And then at the project level, you have shared resources
that the platform team manages, and every app can consume.
These can include things like knowledge for grounding,
sandboxes for your isolated agent compute,
policies for governance and guardrails,
and ability to include and exclude connectors.
Each app has its own workflows, connections, files, and skills.
This is what builders work in day-to-day.
They don't need Azure access anymore,
and so this offers a clear separation
where admins govern the platform,
and developers build on the top.
The platform offers two layers
of governance mapped to two roles.
Layer one is for project.
This is an Azure resource governed by ARM RBAC.
The project admin owns it, and they manage members,
permissions policies quotas, knowledge sandboxes models
scoped at the project level.
Layer two is where developers or builder lives.
They build apps, which includes workflows,
connections, files, and skills.
Here, no Azure access is required;
no Azure permissions are needed.
They consume project-scoped resources within the policies
that the admin set for them.
So as you can clearly see,
one team governs while another team builds,
and both of them inside the same secure boundary.
Building a RAG pipeline today is quite complex.
There are multiple steps involved,
including preparing the vector store and data to be ingested,
and then building the pipeline to parse, chunk,
and tokenize the documents.
We have collapsed this process into few simple steps.
You upload the files.
Logic Apps automatically ingests, chunks,
and vectorizes the content.
There is no pipeline to configure.
There is no infrastructure to maintain by you.
Retrieval is also a native workflow step.
For anyone building grounded, personalized agents,
this dramatically lowers the barrier.
Let me show you how this works.
SPEAKER 1: Here we are in a Logic App where we'll set
up a knowledge base and then use it from an agent in a workflow.
The knowledge base is scoped at the app level,
so you can share it across workflows in the same app.
Before you start, there's a one-time setup.
This capability is built on Cosmos DB as the vector store
and uses Azure OpenAI for models.
That's what we configure here.
You connect the knowledge base to a Cosmos DB instance,
then provide model for embedding generation
and another for chat completions.
Here's an app where I've already completed that setup.
Once configured, you can add files to your knowledge base
and organize them into groups.
The groups are the unit of reference from an agent,
so you can logically group your files based
on the scenario and desired outcome.
When you upload a file, you choose the group it belongs to
and add metadata like name and description.
Since each file goes through tokenization, chunking,
and embedding, we show the status so you know
when it's ready to use.
Here's a workflow with an agent
that classifies incoming documents,
and if it's a contract, then validates
against the organization's approval rules and policies.
Naturally, it needs to be grounded in those rules.
In the agent, you'll see a "Knowledge" section.
The connection is already set up.
Here, you select the specific knowledge group you want
to make available to the agent,
and you can add files directly from this view.
Below that are the instructions guiding the agent's behavior.
Behind the scenes, the agent performs semantic search
and retrieval against your knowledge group based
on the query.
What would normally take significant effort to build
as a custom ingestion
and retrieval pipeline is fully handled for you.
We have uploaded a document classification guide
and contract processing guide for this scenario.
Let's run the workflow with a sample contract.
In the run history, you'll see the agents first classified the
document and identified as a contract.
It then went through the contract validation steps.
All the agent processing and responses are grounded
in the classification and validation document,
with references to knowledge surfaced
in both the agent chat and the run history.
The agent node also shows the specific knowledge group
that was used, along with token utilization,
so you can track usage.
And that's knowledge in Logic Apps.
Now available in public preview.
Give it a try and bring your organization's documents
into your agents without writing a single line of pipeline code.
DIVYA SWARNKAR: Next, I want to talk
about how we are bringing the capabilities
of two Azure services into a cohesive experience.
On the left, we have Azure AI Foundry.
This is the Microsoft's AI platform
where agents are built and hosted.
You define agents with models, tools, instructions,
and you ground the responses in knowledge and enterprise data.
You evaluate, version,
and observe your agent's behavior in Microsoft Foundry.
Foundry is where your agent lives.
On the right, we have Azure Logic Apps.
This becomes your automation and orchestration platform.
This is where agents are invoked and orchestrated.
You trigger agents from any event or schedule using hundreds
of connectors that Logic Apps offers natively.
We bring improved experience
to smoothly use these services together to automate
and operationalize your AI agents and run them
in production at scale.
So let's take a look at this demo where we build agents
in Microsoft Foundry, and we orchestrate and invoke them
from Azure Logic Apps.
All of this is demonstrated
through an auto loan approval process, which allows you
to bring together both deterministic steps as well
as agent reasoning in a single workflow.
SPEAKER 1: Here in Logic Apps,
we start by creating a workflow and adding an agent node.
The agent connects to a Foundry project, and from here,
we can pick any model or existing agent in that project.
See the drop-down.
Every agent in Foundry shows up, ready to invoke.
And if the one we need doesn't exist yet, we can create it
without leaving Logic Apps.
The deep link to Foundry lets us jump
between portals when we need to.
Let's create a new agent right here.
All we need is a name and a model.
Behind the scenes, Logic Apps calls the Foundry APIs
to provision it.
And there it is in our Foundry project.
Let's update the instructions.
Any change we make here flows straight back to Logic Apps.
The agent stays in sync.
Now, a real-world scenario, an auto loan approval workflow
that handles incoming loan requests autonomously.
It runs in real time using a triage agent in Foundry
for duplicate checks, then an auto loan agent
for the approval decision.
With Logic Apps workflows alongside agents,
we combined deterministic business steps
with AI reasoning, which is what most real-world solutions
actually need.
Both agents live in Foundry.
But look at the tools the loan agent is using.
These are native Logic Apps connectors, APIs, and workflows.
That's the unlock.
Foundry as your AI platform and the full Logic Apps ecosystem
with 1,400 plus connectors, your APIs, your custom code,
as your agent's tools, all on a proven enterprise platform.
Let's kick it off by submitting a loan request.
This particular request will need human approval before it
can complete.
In Logic Apps run history, we can see every step
of the workflow with full detail.
Right now, the agent is paused, waiting on human approval.
With Logic Apps workflows, you can build long-running,
human-in-the-loop processes with your Foundry agents.
The approval request lands in Teams.
Once the approval responds, the workflow resumes,
the loan agent finalizes the decision,
and the customer gets their approval notification.
Start to finish, autonomous, with a human
in the loop exactly where it matters.
The run completes, and every step
of the workflow is captured end-to-end:
inputs, outputs, token usage.
This is the operational view your platform
and automation teams need for governance.
In Foundry, you get the agent's own traces and logs,
the reasoning, the tool calls, the thread history.
This is the view your developers need to tune prompts,
debug agent behavior, and track quality over time.
Same execution, two lenses, correlated by run ID
across both portals, so you get the right view
in the right place without losing the thread between them.
DIVYA SWARNKAR: So this brings us towards the end
of this session, and I want to give a quick recap on some
of the key capabilities that I touched in this session today.
We announced Logic Apps Automation, a new platform
for building automations on the same enterprise-grade platform,
but at scale, with low barrier to entry.
We also talked about knowledge as a service
to manage RAG directly inside your workflows.
And finally, we talked about deep integration
between Foundry agents and Logic App workflows for orchestration.
The goal across all three is common.
We want to make AI automation easier to build and easier
to trust in production.
You can learn more about all these announcements
through our documents, blogs, and demos,
which are provided here.
Thank you so much for listening to this session.
I hope you found the content useful, and I can't wait
to see what you build out of these capabilities.
